title: Pauri 9: listening, the gods and scriptures
hook: suniai: by listening even the lowly speak praise, and the scriptures open (Japji 9)

segments.voice: Yesterday, pauri eight and the power of listening. Your line was by listening. Did someone get your full attention, and one more question? Day one hundred seventy-nine.

Most of us know someone who used to have nothing kind to say. The cynic at work. The uncle who complained through every holiday. And then something shifted, maybe a loss, maybe a friendship, maybe just years, and one day you heard them say something generous and were startled. Where did that come from? A new stretch of Japji begins today, pauris nine to fifteen, on listening and then trusting. And pauri nine has an answer for that uncle.
screen: `THE ONE WHO COMPLAINED.` → `ONE DAY, SOMETHING GENEROUS.` → `WHERE DID THAT COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Pauri nine keeps yesterday's drumbeat, suniai, by listening, at the start of every line. Here it is in plain words, following Macauliffe. By listening, Shiva, Brahma and Indra. By listening, even the lowly and the foul-mouthed come to praise. By listening, the ways of yoga and the secrets of the body. By listening, the Shastras, the Smritis and the Vedas. Nanak, the devotees are always in bloom. By listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. Start with the first line. Shiva, Brahma and Indra are great gods in Hindu tradition, and Guru Nanak names them with respect. The pauri places even their greatness inside listening to the Name. Sikhs read this as saying that the One is the source, and all greatness, however high, comes by hearing. Then the line people love: suniai mukh saalaahan mand. Mand means the low, the bad; mukh is the mouth. By listening, even those with bad mouths praise. Nobody is too far gone. Listening, the pauri says, can turn the most bitter tongue toward praise. Then the body: jog jugat tan bhed, the methods of yoga and the hidden workings of the body. And then the scriptures of Guru Nanak's world: Shastras, Smritis, Vedas. By listening, they open. Their meaning isn't locked in the letters; it comes to the one who listens. So this pauri moves from gods, to the worst mouth in the room, to the body, to the books, and says the same thing about each. Whatever is high, whatever is low: the door is listening.
screen: `SHIVA, BRAHMA, INDRA — BY LISTENING.` · `MAND — EVEN THE BAD MOUTH PRAISES.` · `THE BODY'S HIDDEN WAYS.` · `THE SCRIPTURES OPEN.` · then, large: `THE LOWLY SPEAK PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and listen for three sounds around you. The first one, the loudest: name it quietly. The second, softer, something you'd missed until now. And the third, the faintest you can find: a hum, a breath, the air itself. Stay with that third one. Notice how much more you hear when you're looking for it. Then think of one person whose voice you've stopped listening to, and imagine hearing them freshly. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Pauri nine. By listening: the gods, the body's secrets, the scriptures, and even the bad-mouthed come to praise.
Your line: the lowly speak praise. Today, when someone you've written off says something good, hear it, and tell them you heard it. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the ninth pauri each morning as part of Japji's four suniai pauris; each ends with the same refrain, that devotees are always in bloom and listening wipes away pain and wrongdoing.

fork.setup: pauri nine names the gods, then turns to someone else entirely. who?
options: the lowly and the foul-mouthed, who come to praise.
fork.reveal: suniai mukh saalaahan mand: by listening, even bad mouths turn to praise. nobody is too far gone.

original.note: Gurmukhi: by listening, even the bad-mouthed praise (Japji, pauri 9).

trapdoor: what you thought: listening makes you wiser.
what it means: by listening, gods, scriptures and even the worst mouths turn toward praise.
what a scholar hears: Shastras, Smritis and Vedas name the whole range of Brahmanical scripture; the pauri places their opening in hearing the Name.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 9

notes: Pauri 9 paraphrased after Macauliffe; not quoted.
'suniai eesar barmaa ind': eesar read as Shiva. Confirm.
'mukh saalaahan mand': some read 'even the evil praise with their mouths'; others 'the lowly'. Confirm.
Treatment of Hindu deities is respectful and descriptive; the Sikh reading is attributed to Sikhs. Check tone.
